title: Limits with epsilon and N
objectives: Prove that a sequence converges using the epsilon and N definition.

screens.title: Into the band
screens.prose: The dots are $a_n = \tfrac{2n+1}{n+3}$: $\tfrac34, 1, \tfrac76, \tfrac97, \dots$ They creep up towards 2. The shaded band is $2 \pm 0.1$. Drag $N$ along the bottom; the caption reads the gap at the line.
screens.question: Drag $N$ to the first $n$ from which every dot stays strictly inside the band.

hints.text: The gap $|a_n - 2|$ shrinks as $n$ grows. Find where it first drops below 0.1.
Try $n = 47$ and $n = 48$ and read the caption each time.
At 47 the gap is $\tfrac{5}{50} = 0.1$ exactly, which is not inside. At 48 it is $\tfrac{5}{51} \approx 0.0980$.

feedback.correct: Right. From $n = 48$ on, every gap is below 0.1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the gap in the caption and stop at the first one below 0.1.

byKey.edge: At $n = 47$ the gap is exactly 0.1. The dot sits on the edge, and the band needs strictly less.
byKey.late: Every dot from there on is inside, so that line works. A line further left works too; find the first.
byKey.N: Some dots right of your line are still outside the band. Move the line right until the gap is below 0.1.

explain.text: The gap is $|a_n - 2| = \tfrac{5}{n+3}$, which falls as $n$ grows. It equals 0.1 at $n = 47$ and is below 0.1 from $n = 48$. So 48 is the first index that keeps the whole tail inside.

screens.title: Any band you like
screens.prose: Now the band is $2 \pm \varepsilon$, and you choose $\varepsilon$. The dashed line marks the first $n$ from which every dot is inside. Slide $\varepsilon$ from wide to thin.

state.caption: $\varepsilon$ = 0.25: every dot from $n$ = 18 on is inside.

derive.caption: $\varepsilon$ = {{fixed(eps, 2)}}: every dot from $n$ = {{max(1, floor(5 / eps - 3 + 0.000001) + 1)}} on is inside.

screens.question: As $\varepsilon$ shrinks, what happens to the first good $n$?

options.text: It moves right, and for every $\varepsilon$ some $n$ still works.
It stops moving once $\varepsilon$ is small enough.
options.why: You expected a last line. A thinner band always needs a later start here, since the gap $\tfrac{5}{n+3}$ is never 0.

options.text: Below some $\varepsilon$, no $n$ works.
options.why: You expected the band to lose the dots. The gap falls towards 0, so every band catches the tail eventually.

options.text: It moves left.
options.why: You read the slider backwards. A thinner band is harder to enter, so the start comes later.

hints.text: Watch the dashed line as you move $\varepsilon$ from 0.5 to 0.05.
At 0.5 the line is at 8; at 0.05 it is at 98.
The line moves right but never runs out: each $\varepsilon$ has its own $N$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move $\varepsilon$ to 0.05 and to 0.5 and compare where the line sits.

byKey.none: You expected the band to lose the dots. At $\varepsilon = 0.05$ the line is at 98, and the dots after it are inside.

explain.text: Each $\varepsilon$ you chose had its own starting index $N$. That is the meaning of $a_n \to 2$: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $|a_n - 2| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. The order matters: $\varepsilon$ first, then $N$, then every $n \ge N$.

screens.title: The gap as a formula
screens.prose: A proof must handle every $\varepsilon$ at once, so we need the gap as a formula in $n$. Write 2 over the denominator $n + 3$ and subtract.
screens.question: Simplify $|a_n - 2|$ for $a_n = \tfrac{2n+1}{n+3}$.

hints.text: Write $2 = \tfrac{2(n+3)}{n+3} = \tfrac{2n+6}{n+3}$.
The numerator of $a_n - 2$ is $(2n + 1) - (2n + 6)$.
That is $-5$, so $a_n - 2 = \tfrac{-5}{n+3}$. The absolute value drops the sign.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put both terms over $n + 3$ and take the absolute value at the end.

byKey.sign: You found $a_n - 2$. The gap is its absolute value, $\tfrac{5}{n+3}$, which is positive.
byKey.slip: You subtracted $2n + 3$, multiplying only $n$ by 2. Two times $n + 3$ is $2n + 6$.

explain.text: $a_n - 2 = \tfrac{2n + 1 - 2n - 6}{n+3} = \tfrac{-5}{n+3}$. The absolute value is $\tfrac{5}{n+3}$. Check at $n = 47$: $\tfrac{5}{50} = 0.1$, the gap you read on the first screen.

screens.title: Solve for the threshold
screens.prose: We need $\tfrac{5}{n+3} < \varepsilon$. Both sides are positive, so we may take reciprocals and flip the inequality: $\tfrac{n+3}{5} > \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$.
screens.question: The gap is below $\varepsilon$ exactly when $n$ is greater than what? Give it in terms of $\varepsilon$.

hints.text: Multiply $\tfrac{n+3}{5} > \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$ by 5.
That gives $n + 3 > \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon}$.
Subtract 3: $n > \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$.

byKey.flip: You divided $\varepsilon$ by 5. Multiplying $\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$ by 5 gives $\tfrac{5}{\varepsilon}$.
byKey.plus: You added 3. To get $n$ alone from $n + 3$, subtract 3.
byKey.times: You multiplied by $\varepsilon$ instead of dividing. A smaller $\varepsilon$ must give a larger threshold.

explain.text: $\tfrac{5}{n+3} < \varepsilon \iff n + 3 > \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} \iff n > \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$. At $\varepsilon = 0.1$ the threshold is 47, so $n \ge 48$, as you found by dragging. A smaller $\varepsilon$ gives a larger threshold.

screens.title: A thinner band
screens.prose: Take $\varepsilon = 0.01$. The dots are too close together to read by eye now, so we use the threshold $n > \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$.

state.caption: The band $2 \pm 0.01$, with a dot at every 20th $n$.

screens.question: What is the smallest $N$ that works for $\varepsilon = 0.01$?

hints.text: Put $\varepsilon = 0.01$ into $\tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$.
$\tfrac{5}{0.01} - 3 = 497$, and $n$ must be strictly above it.
The first whole number above 497 is 498. Check: $\tfrac{5}{501} \approx 0.00998$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\tfrac{5}{0.01} - 3$, then take the first whole number strictly above it.

byKey.edge: At $n = 497$ the gap is $\tfrac{5}{500} = 0.01$ exactly. The band needs strictly less, so start at 498.
byKey.no-shift: You used $n \ge \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon}$ and dropped the $-3$. The threshold is 497.
byKey.no-shift-1: You solved $n > \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon}$ and dropped the $-3$. The threshold is 497, not 500.
byKey.plus: You added 3 instead of subtracting it. From $n + 3 > 500$, $n > 497$.

explain.text: $n > 497$ gives $N = 498$. At $n = 497$ the gap is $\tfrac{5}{500} = 0.01$ exactly, which fails the strict inequality. Every later $n$ has a smaller gap, since $\tfrac{5}{n+3}$ falls as $n$ grows.

screens.title: Closer every step
screens.prose: A classmate measures $|a_n - 2.5|$ for the same sequence: 1.75, 1.5, 1.33, 1.21, and so on. It shrinks at every single step, for every $n$. So, they say, $a_n \to 2.5$.
screens.question: Is the classmate right?

options.text: No. The gap to 2.5 never drops below 0.5, so $\varepsilon = 0.5$ has no $N$.
Yes. The gap shrinks at every step, so the sequence converges to 2.5.
options.why: You took getting closer for converging. The gap to 2.5 shrinks, but only towards 0.5, never below it.

options.text: Yes. It converges to 2 and to 2.5.
options.why: You allowed two limits. Bands $2 \pm 0.2$ and $2.5 \pm 0.2$ do not overlap, and a tail cannot sit in both.

options.text: No, because the gap does not shrink at every step.
options.why: You doubted the measurements. The gap $0.5 + \tfrac{5}{n+3}$ does fall at every step; the trouble is what it falls to.

hints.text: Write $|a_n - 2.5|$ using $a_n = 2 - \tfrac{5}{n+3}$.
$|a_n - 2.5| = 0.5 + \tfrac{5}{n+3}$, which is always more than 0.5.
So no term is ever inside the band $2.5 \pm 0.5$. That one $\varepsilon$ has no $N$.

feedback.correct: Right. Getting closer is not converging.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the gap to 2.5 falls below every $\varepsilon$, not merely whether it falls.

byKey.yes: You took getting closer for converging. The gap $0.5 + \tfrac{5}{n+3}$ falls, but stays above 0.5, so $\varepsilon = 0.5$ has no $N$.
byKey.both: You allowed two limits. The tail ends inside every band round 2, so it cannot also sit inside a thin band round 2.5.

explain.text: The gap to 2.5 is $0.5 + \tfrac{5}{n+3}$: falling, but never below 0.5. Converging needs the gap to fall below every $\varepsilon$, not merely to fall. The band $2.5 \pm 0.5$ is never entered.

screens.title: The written proof
screens.prose: Assemble the proof that $a_n = \tfrac{2n+1}{n+3} \to 2$ from the pieces you found. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: By the Archimedean property, choose $N \in \mathbb{N}$ with $N > \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$.

lines.why: You fixed one $\varepsilon$. The proof must work for every $\varepsilon > 0$, so it starts from an arbitrary one.
You chose $N$ from $n$. $N$ is fixed before $n$ appears and depends only on $\varepsilon$.

hints.text: The definition's order is $\varepsilon$, then $N$, then $n$.
Choose $N$ from $\varepsilon$ alone, using the threshold $\tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$.
Order: let epsilon, choose N, let n, bound the gap by its value at N, then compare with epsilon.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the definition: $\varepsilon$ first, then $N$, then $n$.

byKey.d1: You fixed $\varepsilon = 0.1$. That proves one band, not every band.
byKey.d2: You used $N = n + 1$. Then $n \ge N$ is false, and $N$ depends on $n$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Archimedes gives a whole number $N$ above $\tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$. For $n \ge N$ the gap is at most its value at $N$, which is below $\varepsilon$. Nothing in the choice of $N$ mentions $n$.

screens.title: An $N$ that moves
screens.prose: This proof claims $(-1)^n \to 1$. The claim is false: the odd terms are $-1$. So some line must break the definition.
screens.question: Which line breaks the definition?

options.text: Line 3: $N$ is chosen from $n$. $N$ must come before $n$ and depend only on $\varepsilon$.
Line 1: $\varepsilon$ should be a fixed number such as 0.1.
options.why: You fixed $\varepsilon$. The definition needs every $\varepsilon$, so 'let $\varepsilon > 0$' is right.
You computed for an odd $N$. Here $N = 2n$ is even, so $(-1)^N = 1$ and line 4 is true.

options.text: No line: the claim is true.
options.why: You accepted the proof. The odd terms are $-1$, at distance 2 from 1, so $\varepsilon = 1$ fails for every $N$.

hints.text: In the definition, which comes first: $N$ or $n$?
Line 3 builds $N$ out of $n$.
$N$ must be fixed from $\varepsilon$ before any $n$ is named.

feedback.correct: Right. An $N$ built from $n$ is not the definition's $N$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the order of the choices against the definition.

byKey.none: You accepted the proof. Fix any $N$: the odd $n$ beyond it give $|(-1)^n - 1| = 2$.

explain.text: With $n = 3$ the proof picks $N = 6$, which says nothing about odd terms past 6. Once $N$ is fixed first, the odd terms beyond it sit 2 away from 1. So no $N$ works for $\varepsilon = 1$.

screens.title: A wide band
screens.prose: At $\varepsilon = 2$ the threshold $\tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$ is $-0.5$, and every $n \ge 1$ already works. But $N$ must be an index, at least 1. So the proof takes a whole number $N$ above both 1 and $\tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$.
screens.question: Write 'above both 1 and $\tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$' as above one expression in $\varepsilon$.

hints.text: A number above both $a$ and $b$ is above the larger of the two.
The larger of $a$ and $b$ is written $\max(a, b)$.
So $N$ is a whole number above $\max(1, \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Being above both numbers means being above the larger one.

byKey.min: You took the smaller of the two. A number above the smaller one can still be below the larger.
byKey.thr: You dropped the 1. At $\varepsilon = 2$ that bound is $-0.5$, and 0 is above it but is not an index.

explain.text: For $\varepsilon \ge 1.25$ the threshold is at most 1, and the max is 1. Below 1.25 the threshold takes over. The proof needs a valid $N$, not the smallest, so starting above 1 costs nothing.

screens.title: No band holds it
screens.prose: $b_n = (-1)^n$ jumps between $-1$ and 1. To show it has no limit $L$, we negate the definition, as in the proof course. Swap each quantifier and negate the inequality.

state.caption: A band $L \pm 1$ with $L = 0.6$: the dots at $-1$ fall outside.

screens.question: Which statement says $b_n \not\to L$?

options.text: There is an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every $N$, some $n \ge N$ has $|b_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$.
For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $N$, every $n \ge N$ has $|b_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$.
options.why: You asked every term to be far from $L$. One far term past each $N$ is enough; with $L = 1$, half the terms equal 1.

options.text: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $|b_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$.
options.why: You negated only the inequality. Negation also turns 'for every' into 'there is', and back.

options.text: There is an $n$ with $|b_n - L| \ge 1$.
options.why: You found one far term. A single far term says nothing about the tail; it must recur past every $N$.

hints.text: The definition reads: for every $\varepsilon$, there is $N$, for all $n \ge N$, the gap is below $\varepsilon$.
Negating gives: there is $\varepsilon$, for every $N$, there is $n \ge N$, the gap is at least $\varepsilon$.
Take $\varepsilon = 1$: $-1$ and 1 are 2 apart, so they cannot both lie within 1 of $L$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate each quantifier in turn, then the inequality.

byKey.ineq-only: You negated only the inequality. 'For every $\varepsilon$, there is $N$' must become 'there is $\varepsilon$, for every $N$'.

explain.text: Take $\varepsilon = 1$. Whatever $L$ is, $-1$ and 1 are 2 apart, so one of them is at least 1 from $L$. Past any $N$ both values recur, so some $n \ge N$ is outside the band.

screens.title: The threshold as code
screens.prose: Write `smallest_n(eps)`: the smallest $N$ with $\tfrac{5}{n+3} < \varepsilon$ for every $n \ge N$. Use exact `Fraction` arithmetic, so a gap equal to $\varepsilon$ is never mistaken for one below it.
screens.question: Complete the function.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction
import math

def smallest_n(eps):
    """Smallest N with 5/(n + 3) < eps for every n >= N."""
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. They cover six values of epsilon, two where a gap equals epsilon exactly, and a tiny epsilon. The answer must be an int.

hints.text: The proof's threshold is $t = \tfrac{5}{\varepsilon} - 3$, and $n$ must be strictly above it.
The first whole number above $t$ is `math.floor(t) + 1`.
Return `max(1, math.floor(t) + 1)`, with `t` built from `Fraction(eps)`.

feedback.correct: Right. Exact arithmetic gets the boundary cases.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the threshold exactly with `Fraction`, take the first whole number above it, and keep it at least 1.

explain.text: `math.floor(t) + 1` is the first whole number strictly above $t$, even when $t$ is whole, as at $\varepsilon = \tfrac{1}{10}$. At $\varepsilon = \tfrac{5}{51}$ the gap at $n = 48$ is exactly $\varepsilon$, so the answer is 49. The `max` keeps $N \ge 1$ for wide bands.

screens.title: Pick the accuracy
screens.prose: A desk prices an option on an $n$-step binomial tree. Its error is below $\tfrac{3}{n}$ pence. A client wants the price to within 0.01p.

state.caption: The error bound against the number of tree steps.

screens.question: What is the smallest number of steps the bound guarantees?

hints.text: Here $\varepsilon = 0.01$ and the gap is $\tfrac{3}{n}$.
The first whole number above 300 is 301.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $\tfrac{3}{n} < 0.01$ for $n$ and take the first whole number above.

byKey.edge: At 300 steps the bound is $\tfrac{3}{300} = 0.01$ exactly, not below it. Take 301.
byKey.tenth: You solved for 0.1p. The client asked for 0.01p, ten times finer.
byKey.pounds: You converted to pounds. The bound and the target are both in pence.

explain.text: $\tfrac{3}{n} < 0.01$ needs $n > 300$, so $N = 301$. The client names $\varepsilon$ and the desk answers with $N$. The definition of a limit is exactly 'pick the accuracy, I give you the step count'.

ideas: $a_n \to L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. $N$ may depend on $\varepsilon$, never on $n$.
To prove it, simplify $|a_n - L|$, solve $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for $n$, and choose $N$ above that threshold by Archimedes.
To disprove it, find one $\varepsilon$ that leaves terms outside the band beyond every $N$, as $\varepsilon = 1$ does for $(-1)^n$.
summary.trap: Getting closer to 2.5 at every step is not converging to 2.5: the gap must fall below every $\varepsilon$.

quiz.prose: Two students write the definition of $a_n \to L$.
quiz.question: Which one is the definition?

options.text: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$.
There is $N$ such that for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$.
options.why: You put $N$ first. One $N$ for every $\varepsilon$ forces $a_n = L$ for all $n \ge N$.

options.text: There is $\varepsilon > 0$ and $N$ with $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$.
options.why: You asked for one band. Every bounded sequence fits in some wide band.

options.text: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $n$ with $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$.
options.why: You asked for one close term. The whole tail must be close, not one term.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which choice comes first and how many terms must be close.

explain.text: $\varepsilon$ is chosen first, by a sceptic. $N$ may then depend on it. Every term from $N$ on must be inside the band.

quiz.prose: The constant sequence $c_n = 7$ for every $n$, with $L = 7$ and $\varepsilon = 0.001$.
quiz.question: Which $N$ works?

options.text: Every $N \ge 1$.
Only $N \ge 1000$.
options.why: You expected a thin band to need a late start. Every term is exactly 7, so the gap is 0 from the first term.

options.text: None, since the terms never get closer to 7.
options.why: You looked for getting closer. The gap is already 0, which is below every $\varepsilon$.

options.text: Only $N = 7$.
options.why: You matched the value 7 with the index. The index and the limit are different things.

feedback.correct: Right. The gap is 0 for every term.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $|c_n - 7|$ for any $n$.

explain.text: $|c_n - 7| = 0 < \varepsilon$ for every $n$. So any $N$ works, for every $\varepsilon$. A constant sequence converges to its value.

quiz.question: What is the smallest $N$ that works for $\varepsilon = 0.05$?

byKey.edge: At $n = 59$ the gap is $\tfrac{3}{60} = 0.05$ exactly, not below it.
byKey.no-shift: You solved $n > 60$. The condition is $n + 1 > 60$, so $n > 59$.

options.text: $a_n \to 0$: the gap is $\tfrac1n$, below $\varepsilon$ for every $n > \tfrac1\varepsilon$.
It diverges, because the sign keeps changing.
options.why: You took the sign changes for divergence. The gap to 0 is $\tfrac1n$, which falls below any $\varepsilon$.

options.text: It has no limit, because it is not getting closer at every step.
options.why: You required steady approach. The definition asks only that the tail stay in the band.

options.text: $a_n \to 1$, its largest size.
options.why: You took the first size for the limit. $|a_n - 1| \ge \tfrac12$ for every $n \ge 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the gap $|a_n - 0|$.

explain.text: $|a_n - 0| = \tfrac1n$, so any $N > \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$ works. The signs alternate, but the band round 0 holds both signs. Convergence needs no monotone approach.
